newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan envoy says rebel deaths may inhibit attacks.
newsitem.headline: Japan envoy says rebel deaths may inhibit attacks.

text.p: Japan's ambassador to Peru, Morihisa Aoki, said on Thursday that the death of all 14 Marxist rebels who held 72 hostages at his residence in Lima would help prevent similar terrorist attacks.
"The fact that all the terrorists died will make it difficult (for other terrorists) to resort to similar attacks," Aoki said. "It was a big achievement.
"Our time spent there as hostages was not wasted," he told a news conference after meeting with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

In a spectacular rescue operation, Peruvian troops stormed Aoki's home in Lima on April 22, killing all 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels. All but one of the 72 hostages held for 126 days were freed alive.
The Cuban-inspired rebels took over Aoki's residence on December 17 during a lavish reception celebrating the birthday of Japanese Emperor Akihito.
The silver-haired Aoki, 58, declined to say if he would retire from his diplomatic career.
"I am not entitled to say myself whether or not to resign. I must wait for my boss' judgement," Aoki said.
Aoki denied that a security lapse allowed the heavily armed rebels to seize his residence for four months.
"Even if we had brought in security police armed with guns, how could they have pushed the rebels back?" he said.
"A shoot-out might have broken out at the beginning and more people might have been killed," he added.
The Marxist rebels initially took some 500 people hostage and then gradually released most of them, although 72, mainly VIPs, remained in captivity.
Aoki quoted some of the hostage-takers as telling him that they decided to storm Japan's diplomatic mission because a large number of VIPs visited there.
The Marxist rebels' main demand was the release of jailed comrades, but they also used the siege to protest against poverty in Peru.
Aoki said he successfully sent a "secret" letter on April 3 to Japanese authorities warning that the hostage situation was becoming serious.
"The hostages' patience is nearing its limits. If the hostages are held here for any longer, unexpected things could happen," Aoki quoted the letter as saying.
